passages.happening:
‘For behold, the day is coming, burning like a furnace, when all the arrogant and every evildoer will be stubble’ (verse 1). Not a root or branch will be left to them.

‘But for you who fear My name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, and you will go out and leap like calves from the stall’ (verse 2). On the day God is preparing, the wicked will be like ashes under the feet of those who fear him (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
In Hebrew Bibles these verses are the end of chapter 3, and they finish the argument that began when some said it was futile to serve God. The same day is a furnace for the arrogant and a sunrise for the faithful. Those who seemed to prosper are burned like stubble, and those who seemed to lose come out into the light.

The winged sun disk was a well-known symbol across the ancient Near East, used in Egyptian and Persian art for divine or royal protection, and stamped on storage jar handles in Judah in Hezekiah's time. Malachi takes that familiar picture and gives it to righteousness itself, rising on the faithful like morning. The calves are young animals let out after a winter penned in the stall, a farmer's picture of pure joy.
passages.later: Isaiah promised, ‘Arise, shine, for your light has come’ (Isaiah 60:1). A psalm calls God himself a sun: ‘For the LORD God is a sun and a shield’ (Psalm 84:11).
passages.hard:
How should the picture of the wicked as ashes under the feet of the faithful be read?

It is a picture of God's justice made visible on his day, given to people who were tempted to think evil always wins. It is God who sets the arrogant ablaze; the faithful do not take vengeance, and the verse gives no one a warrant to harm anyone now. The prophets speak this way to comfort the oppressed, not to invite them to gloat. Elsewhere God says, ‘I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked’ (Ezekiel 33:11).
passages.asks: The same day is a furnace for some and a sunrise for others. Ask what this chapter says makes the difference. And ask what it would mean to live now in the light of that dawn.

passages.t: Remember Moses, and watch for Elijah
passages.happening: ‘Remember the law of My servant Moses, the statutes and ordinances I commanded him for all Israel at Horeb’ (verse 4). ‘Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD’ (verse 5). ‘And he will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers’ (verse 6). Otherwise God will come and strike the land with a curse.
passages.hearers:
These verses close not only Malachi but the whole book of the Twelve, and many scholars think the collection of the Prophets too. They look back to Moses and forward to Elijah. Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, where the law was given.

The hope of Elijah's return grew from the way his life on earth ended: he did not die but was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind. By Jesus' day, the scribes taught that Elijah must come first. Elijah remains present in Jewish practice: a cup is set out for him at the Passover meal. And in synagogue reading it became the custom to repeat verse 5 after verse 6, so that the prophets would not end on the word curse.

In a Christian Bible these are the last words of the Old Testament. The next voice is Matthew's, and within three chapters a man dressed like Elijah is preaching by the Jordan.
passages.later: The angel said that John would go ‘in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children’ (Luke 1:17). Jesus said of John, ‘he is the Elijah who was to come’ (Matthew 11:14), and ‘Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him’ (Matthew 17:12).
passages.hard:
Was John the Baptist literally Elijah, and is Elijah still to come?

Jesus says John is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:12), yet when John was asked, ‘Are you Elijah?’ he answered, ‘I am not’ (John 1:21). Most interpreters reconcile the two through Luke 1:17: John was not Elijah returned in person, but he came in Elijah's spirit and power and did the work Malachi described.

Christians differ on whether the promise has a further fulfillment, and this site takes no side. Some point to Jesus' words, ‘Elijah does indeed come, and he will restore all things’ (Matthew 17:11), as a sign that an Elijah-like ministry will come before Christ's return. Others read Matthew 17:11-12 as saying the promise was fulfilled in John. Jewish tradition still waits for Elijah as the herald of the Messiah. On every Christian reading, John the Baptist is the one the Gospels present as Malachi's messenger.
passages.asks: Elijah's work is to turn the hearts of fathers and children toward each other. Ask which relationship in your family most needs that turning. And if your own father was absent or distant, ask what it means that God named this healing as part of his coming.
